scenes.text: This is Countersign. A second signature, before any code change that moves money goes live.
Here's the problem. A code change can pass every single test, and still send the wrong amount of money. A nine hundred rupee refund goes out as ninety thousand.
Countersign checks every pull request that touches money. This is the payments lead's view, at a sample company. Rohan, a developer, has two changes waiting on the refund API.
In the first, Rohan switches the amount field from paise to rupees. He updates the mobile app too, and every normal test passes. Most teams would merge this.

Countersign's first question: who will break? Nobody labels what each app sends, so it works that out from recorded requests. Two apps still send paise. Even the standard API checker said this change was fine.

Second question: is the money right? It replays last week's four thousand, one hundred and eighty refunds through the new code. Eight hundred and ninety come out wrong. For every one, it can show exactly what the app sent, and what the bank would be told to pay.
So Countersign stops the change, and the merge button stays locked. There are two ways forward.
If it's a mistake, fix it. Rohan makes the unit explicit, with paise as the default. Countersign checks again. Every app works, every refund is right, and the merge unlocks.

But some changes are meant to move money differently. Finance wants refunds above one lakh rupees reviewed by a person. Countersign stops this one too. Seven of last week's refunds, ten lakh rupees in all, would be turned away.
Here, nothing needs fixing. Someone has to decide. Ananya, the payments lead, reads the numbers, countersigns that exact commit, and gives her reason. Only then does the change merge.
Every decision goes into the audit log. What was checked, what it found, who signed, and why.
Now the real thing. Countersign runs as a GitHub Action. Here is the same change as a pull request on GitHub, and the line that changes paise to rupees.
GitHub runs two checks on it. The normal tests pass. Then Countersign runs, and fails.
It posts its report right on the pull request: a nine hundred rupee refund would go out as ninety thousand. And GitHub blocks the merge.
Now the fix is pushed. GitHub runs both checks again, on the new commit. This time, both pass.
Countersign updates the same comment to all clear, and GitHub lets the change merge.
